Electricity—Electric Potential III (Electric Field from the Potential)
We know from previous lessons that we have a relationship between the electric potential and the electric field. Recall that this relationship was expressed as

Let's look at a few examples of this. Firstly, one can conceptually understand that if we choose the closed loop to be on an equipotential surface, V doesn't change along the surface and so 
ΔV = 0.
Secondly, we look at a closed path of the shape seen below.
A small circle labeled + represents a point charge. Six arrows begin at evenly spaced points on the circle (60° apart) and extend radially outward. A dashed blue circle centered on the charge is labeled r = r1. A larger dashed blue circle, also centered on the charge, is labeled r = r2. A directed path consists of four segments shown as red arrows.
Segment 1 begins at a point on the inner (r1) circle and extends radially outward, ending at a point on the outer (r2) circle.
Segment 2 begins at the endpoint of segment 1 and continues on the outer circle, forming an arc of approximately 50°.
Segment 3 begins on the outer circle at the endpoint of segment 2 and extends radially inward, ending at a point on the inner circle.
Segment 4 begins at the endpoint of segment 3 and continues on the inner circle, ending at the starting point of segment 1.

Yes! Let's add all the segments up.
Adding all these up, we get
ΔVloop = segment 1 + segment 2 + segment 3 + segment 4
ΔVloop = 𝜆 + 0 − 𝜆 − 0
ΔVloop = 0
Although we won't prove it here, it can be shown that any closed path near a single charged particle will give a potential difference of zero. Since electric potential obeys superposition, if the closed path integral is zero for one charge, it will be zero for any distribution of charges. The fact that ΔV over a closed path is zero reflects that electric forces are conservative, and that the potential difference between any two points does not depend on the path.

Part 1 of 8 - Conceptualize
An electric dipole in an external electric field behaves like a needle mounted at its midpoint on a vertical pivot. The dipole can be forced to another orientation by exerting a torque on it to move it from its position of lowest energy. When released, it will oscillate like a torsional pendulum. The electric dipole in this problem is small in size like one that might be used in a classroom experiment. The dipole moment will be in the picocoulomb-meter range and the torque, which tends to turn it clockwise to align it with the field, will be on the order of a few nanonewton-meters, with the potential energy on the order of nanojoules. In the orientation described, the dipole is close to its maximum potential energy since its moment is close to being opposite the field direction.
An electric dipole lies on an x y coordinate plane in an external electric field labeled vector E that points down and right. The negative charge of the dipole is in the fourth quadrant and the positive charge is in the second quadrant. Vector p points from the negative charge up and left to the positive charge and is nearly antiparallel to the electric field.
Part 2 of 8 - Categorize
We use the definition of dipole moment and the equation for torque exerted on a dipole by an electric field. We compute the dot product of the moment and the electric field vectors to find the potential energy and compute the maximum potential energy for the dipole when its moment is opposite in direction to the electric field.
